findings.title: No runtime duckdb version guard for offset-derived layout
findings.description: extract_connection_ptr hardcodes the +16 pybind11 header offset and the +32 DuckDBPyConnection member offset, but the docstring states these are 'Validated on duckdb 1.3.2' only. CLAUDE.md declares the supported range as duckdb>=1.3.2,<1.6, so the code is expected to run on 1.4.x and 1.5.x where the DuckDBPyConnection member layout could have changed. Nothing in the function reads duckdb.__version__ or otherwise compares the running version against the one the offsets were validated for. The only mitigation is the docstring sentence 'Re-verify offsets when upgrading duckdb' (line 34), which is a comment, not an enforced mechanism. On an unvalidated-but-supported version the code will silently read a wrong member offset.
findings.impact: A user installing any 1.4/1.5 duckdb wheel within the declared supported range gets no signal that the offsets are unverified for their version; the bridge either silently produces a wrong pointer or crashes (see PBR-DES-3), with no indication that a layout migration is the cause.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit version guard: read duckdb.__version__ and compare against a small set/range of versions whose offsets have actually been verified. On a non-validated version, either raise a clear error or emit a warning instructing the user to re-verify offsets, and centralize the verified-version constant so it is a single source of truth alongside the offsets. At minimum, gate the offsets behind a per-version lookup so an unknown version fails loudly rather than using 1.3.2 numbers blindly.

findings.title: No graceful failure path: layout drift segfaults instead of raising
findings.description: After reading cpp_obj_p at id+16 (line 59) the code immediately dereferences cpp_obj_p+32 (line 62) and then passes conn_ptr into duckdb_query (line 67) with no NULL/sanity check on either intermediate pointer. If the pybind11/struct layout assumptions break on a newer duckdb (the exact scenario the docstring warns about), cpp_obj_p can come back NULL or garbage, making ctypes.c_void_p.from_address(cpp_obj_p + 32) read near-NULL/arbitrary memory, and conn_ptr can be a bogus address handed straight to the C API. The intended safety net, the SELECT 1 validation query, only catches pointers that survive a full query and return DuckDBError; a NULL or wild pointer dereferenced inside duckdb_query segfaults the process instead. So the 'graceful failure path when the layout changes' that this review focuses on does not actually exist for the most likely failure modes.
findings.impact: On layout drift the library hard-crashes the interpreter (SIGSEGV) rather than raising a catchable Python exception, giving the user no actionable error and no clean recovery.
findings.recommendation: Insert cheap defensive guards that convert the common failure modes into a RuntimeError: check `if not cpp_obj_p:` before computing cpp_obj_p+32, and `if not conn_ptr:` before calling duckdb_query. These turn the NULL/zero cases (the most probable result of a shifted offset) into a clean exception, dramatically narrowing the segfault window the docstring already acknowledges.

findings.title: Magic offset literals inline with no named constants
findings.description: The two load-bearing layout constants (16 for the CPython/pybind11 header, 32 for the unique_ptr<Connection> member) are written as bare literals embedded in from_address expressions. Their meaning lives only in the docstring (lines 22-27). There is no named constant tying the literal to its derivation, so a maintainer re-verifying offsets for a new duckdb release must edit values inside expressions and keep the prose in sync by hand. This is exactly the kind of duplicated-truth that the 'Re-verify offsets' follow-up requires touching.
findings.impact: Increases the chance that a re-verification updates the docstring but not the code (or vice versa), and makes the fragile constants harder to locate and audit.
findings.recommendation: Hoist the offsets to module-level named constants (e.g. PYOBJECT_HEADER_SIZE = 16, CONNECTION_MEMBER_OFFSET = 32) with the derivation comment attached, and reference them in the from_address calls so the offsets have a single, self-documenting source of truth.

findings.title: Validation RuntimeError lacks diagnostic context
findings.description: When the round-trip validation fails, the helper raises RuntimeError('extracted connection pointer failed validation') with no context: it does not report the running duckdb version, the offsets used, or the most likely cause (an unvalidated layout). Given the function's own docstring identifies version-dependent layout as the primary failure mode, the error is the natural place to surface that hypothesis to the user.
findings.impact: A user hitting this on a newer duckdb gets a generic message and no pointer toward the actual root cause (offset/layout drift), slowing diagnosis of precisely the fragility this code is most exposed to.
findings.recommendation: Include duckdb.__version__ and a hint to re-verify the pybind11/struct offsets in the RuntimeError message (e.g. mention the validated version and that the layout may have changed for the running version).

notes: Focus answer: pybridge.py has NO version guard, NO re-verify mechanism beyond a docstring sentence (line 34), and NO graceful failure path. The supported range (duckdb>=1.3.2,<1.6 per CLAUDE.md) is wider than the validated version (1.3.2 only, line 31), so versions inside the declared range run on unverified offsets. The SELECT 1 round-trip is the only safety net and it only catches pointers that survive a query and return DuckDBError; NULL/wild pointers from a shifted offset segfault instead (architecture note bridge.md section 6 items 1-3 corroborate). Highest-leverage fixes: a duckdb.__version__ guard (PBR-DES-1) plus cheap NULL guards to make failure catchable (PBR-DES-3).
